title: The Hallmarks of Aging
description: Lopez-Otin's organising framework, from the 2013 nine to the 2023 twelve

concepts.title: The 2013 Synthesis: Nine Hallmarks
concepts.contentHtml:
In 2013, Carlos Lopez-Otin, Maria Blasco, Linda Partridge, Manuel Serrano, and Guido Kroemer published The Hallmarks of Aging in Cell — a deliberate echo of Hanahan and Weinberg's cancer framework. Their goal was to extract from a sprawling literature a small set of cellular and molecular processes that, taken together, characterise the aged state and whose modulation can change lifespan or healthspan.

The original nine: genomic instability, telomere attrition, epigenetic alterations, loss of proteostasis, deregulated nutrient sensing, mitochondrial dysfunction, cellular senescence, stem cell exhaustion, and altered intercellular communication. Each was admitted to the list only if it satisfied three criteria: it appears with normal aging, experimental aggravation accelerates aging, and experimental amelioration extends healthspan.

The framework reorganised the field. A drug that activates AMPK (metformin) and one that inhibits mTOR (rapamycin) both target deregulated nutrient sensing; senolytics target cellular senescence; rejuvenation factors in young plasma target altered intercellular communication. The hallmarks turned aging from a heterogeneous list of phenotypes into a finite set of druggable nodes.

concepts.title: The 2023 Update: Twelve Hallmarks
concepts.contentHtml:
The 2023 revision (Lopez-Otin et al., Cell) added three new hallmarks reflecting a decade of mechanistic and clinical evidence: disabled macroautophagy (separated from general proteostasis loss because age-related decline of autophagic flux is independently sufficient to drive phenotypes), chronic inflammation ("inflammaging" — sustained low-grade NF-kB activation, IL-6 and TNF elevation), and dysbiosis (age-related shifts in gut microbiome composition that feed back on immunity, metabolism and brain).

The expanded list also reclassified the hallmarks into primary (causes of damage: genomic instability, telomere attrition, epigenetic alterations, loss of proteostasis, disabled macroautophagy), antagonistic (initially compensatory but harmful when chronic: deregulated nutrient sensing, mitochondrial dysfunction, cellular senescence), and integrative (the system-level phenotypes that ultimately produce frailty: stem cell exhaustion, altered intercellular communication, chronic inflammation, dysbiosis).

This taxonomy matters causally. Primary hallmarks should ideally be prevented; antagonistic hallmarks should be modulated rather than eliminated (mild senescence and mTOR signalling are useful in development); integrative hallmarks are downstream and may be the easiest to read out as biomarkers.

concepts.title: Gompertz Mortality and Aging as a Disease
concepts.contentHtml:
Aging at the population level obeys Benjamin Gompertz's 1825 law: the per-capita mortality rate m(t) rises exponentially with age, m(t) = A·exp(B·t), with a characteristic mortality doubling time of about 8 years in adult humans. Healthspan and lifespan are both governed by this exponential. A drug that shifts the curve down by a factor of two buys roughly 8 years of life expectancy; one that flattens the slope (reduces B) is genuinely 'anti-aging' rather than merely life-extending at the population level.

$$m(t) = A\,e^{B t}, \quad B \approx \ln(2)/8\,\text{yr}^{-1}$$

The Lopez-Otin programme treats the hallmarks as the molecular substrate of B. If chronic inflammation, senescent cell burden, and proteostatic collapse are what make 80-year-old tissue fail more often than 40-year-old tissue, then directly targeting them is, mechanistically, anti-aging medicine.

This logic underwrites the policy push to recognise aging itself as an indication. As of the 2024-2025 FDA discussions (Bredesen, Barzilai, and others), there is still no formal acceptance of 'aging' as a disease label, but the agency has signalled openness to multi-morbidity endpoints — composite outcomes covering several age-related diseases simultaneously. The TAME trial (next lesson) was designed around exactly this idea.

title: Telomere Biology and Replicative Senescence
description: Hayflick, telomerase, shelterin, and the end-protection problem

concepts.title: The Hayflick Limit, Revisited
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1961, Leonard Hayflick and Paul Moorhead showed that normal human fibroblasts in culture undergo a finite number of divisions — roughly ~50 population doublings — before entering an irreversible non-dividing state, against the prevailing Carrel dogma that cells were intrinsically immortal. The phenomenon is now called the Hayflick limit, and the terminal state is replicative senescence.

$$\text{Hayflick limit} \;\approx\; 50\;\text{population doublings (human fibroblasts)}$$

The molecular cause was elusive until 1990s work on telomeres. Each round of DNA replication leaves a small unreplicated overhang at the lagging-strand 3' end (the end-replication problem), so chromosome ends shorten by ~50-100 bp per division. Once any single telomere reaches a critically short threshold, ATM/ATR sense the unprotected end as a double-strand break, p53 is stabilised, p21 is induced, and the cell enters senescence.

Two important caveats. First, the limit is set by the shortest telomere, not the average — a useful fact for diagnostics. Second, in vivo human stem cells maintain low telomerase activity that partially offsets shortening, so the strict ~50 doublings of cultured fibroblasts is a ceiling, not the rate at which telomeres deplete in real tissue.

concepts.title: Telomerase and the 2009 Nobel
concepts.contentHtml:
Telomerase is a ribonucleoprotein reverse transcriptase that extends the 3' G-rich strand using its own internal RNA template. Its discovery is one of the cleanest stories in modern biology. Elizabeth Blackburn (with grad student Carol Greider) found in 1984, in Tetrahymena, an enzyme that added TTGGGG repeats to a synthetic substrate. Jack Szostak earlier showed that yeast linear plasmids are stabilised by Tetrahymena telomeric DNA — proving telomeres are functionally interchangeable across phyla. The three shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

The human enzyme has two essential subunits: hTERT (the catalytic protein) and hTR (the RNA template, encoded by TERC). Telomerase is active in germline, embryonic stem cells, and a small subset of activated lymphocytes and stem cells; it is silenced in most somatic tissue. Re-expression of hTERT alone is sufficient to immortalise primary human fibroblasts (Bodnar et al., 1998) — a foundational result for the field.

Loss-of-function variants in TERT, TERC, or shelterin components cause the telomere biology disorders: dyskeratosis congenita (very short telomeres in childhood), idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, and aplastic anaemia. These are essentially natural human knockouts proving that telomere maintenance is rate-limiting for tissue renewal.

concepts.title: Shelterin and the End-Protection Problem
concepts.contentHtml:
Telomeric DNA alone is inert; the shelterin complex distinguishes a chromosome end from a broken DNA end and prevents inappropriate repair. Six proteins: TRF1, TRF2 (bind double-stranded TTAGGG repeats), POT1 (binds single-stranded 3' overhang), TPP1 (bridges POT1 and TIN2 and recruits telomerase), TIN2, and RAP1.

Shelterin folds the telomeric overhang back into a t-loop by strand invasion of the duplex tract, hiding the 3' end. This sequesters it from ATM (TRF2-suppressed) and ATR (POT1-suppressed) damage signalling, and from non-homologous end joining (which would fuse chromosomes end-to-end). Acute TRF2 loss produces dramatic chromosome fusion trains in metaphase spreads.

The clinical relevance ties back to senescence and cancer: when telomeres get short enough that shelterin cannot maintain a stable t-loop, ATM fires and the cell senesces (in normal cells) or — if p53 is also disabled — proceeds into crisis, a phase of massive end-to-end fusions and breakage-fusion-bridge cycles that often spawn the karyotypic chaos of advanced tumours. Reactivation of telomerase, or rarely the alternative-lengthening-of-telomeres (ALT) pathway, is what eventually rescues a cell from crisis to immortality.

title: Cellular Senescence and Senolytics
description: SASP, p16/p21, and the in vivo evidence for clearing senescent cells

concepts.title: What Senescence Actually Is
concepts.contentHtml:
Cellular senescence is a stable proliferative arrest accompanied by a distinctive secretory program. Critically it is not just "old cell". A senescent cell is metabolically active, resistant to apoptosis (often via BCL-2 / BCL-XL upregulation), enlarged and flattened, with persistent DNA damage foci, and stained by SA-beta-galactosidase at pH 6 — the textbook histochemical marker.

The molecular gatekeepers are the cyclin-dependent-kinase inhibitors p16^{INK4a} (encoded with p14^{ARF} at the CDKN2A locus) and p21^{CIP1} (encoded by CDKN1A). p21 is the rapid, p53-driven response to acute damage; p16 accumulates more slowly and enforces the long-term arrest. Cdkn2a expression is one of the most reliable single-gene biomarkers of biological age in mice.

Senescence has at least three triggers in vivo: replicative (telomere-driven, lesson 2), oncogene-induced (e.g., HRAS-G12V activation in primary cells triggers OIS via the p16-RB and p53 axes — a critical anti-tumour response), and stress-induced premature senescence from oxidative damage, irradiation, or chemotherapy. The same molecular endpoint serves three quite different physiological purposes — tumour suppression, wound healing, and as we will see, age-related decline.

concepts.title: The SASP and the Bystander Problem
concepts.contentHtml:
The defining feature of senescent cells in tissue is the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), characterised by Judith Campisi's lab in the late 2000s. Senescent cells secrete a complex cocktail of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-8, IL-1alpha), chemokines (CXCL1, CCL2), growth factors, and matrix remodellers (MMP-3, MMP-9). The transcriptional master regulator is NF-kB, with C/EBPbeta and mTOR-dependent translation as required co-conspirators.

The SASP turns a small senescent population into a paracrine wrecking crew. Bystander cells receive sustained inflammatory signalling, accumulate DNA damage, and themselves enter senescence — a positive feedback that explains why senescent burden grows non-linearly with age. SASP factors also degrade extracellular matrix, recruit suppressive myeloid cells, and in some contexts promote rather than suppress neighbouring cancer cell proliferation. Senescence is therefore antagonistically pleiotropic in the Williams sense: useful early (tumour suppression, wound repair), harmful late (chronic inflammation, fibrosis, frailty).

Crucially, only a small percentage of cells in old tissue are senescent. Estimates from immunostaining and single-cell RNA-seq put the number at roughly 1-15% in old human tissue, depending on tissue and assay. The disproportionate effect comes from the SASP amplifier, which is the rationale for clearance rather than suppression as a therapeutic strategy.

concepts.title: In Vivo Clearance and the First Senolytics
concepts.contentHtml:
The decisive experiment was Darren Baker, Jan van Deursen and colleagues' 2011 paper in Nature. They engineered a mouse (INK-ATTAC) carrying an FK506-binding-protein-Caspase-8 transgene driven by the p16^{INK4a} promoter, so that any p16-high cell could be ablated on demand by giving the synthetic dimeriser AP20187. In a progeroid BubR1-hypomorph background, lifelong clearance of p16-positive cells delayed sarcopenia, cataracts and adipose loss. A 2016 follow-up extended the result to naturally aged mice and increased median lifespan ~25%.

This proved that senescent cells cause phenotypes of aging, not merely correlate with them. It motivated the search for small molecules that selectively kill senescent cells — senolytics. Mayo Clinic groups (James Kirkland, Tamar Tchkonia) showed that senescent cells depend on specific anti-apoptotic 'SCAPs' (senescent cell anti-apoptotic pathways): the combination dasatinib + quercetin (D+Q) hits PI3K/SRC-family and BCL-2-family dependencies and clears senescent adipocytes and endothelial cells in mice and, in pilot trials, humans with diabetic kidney disease. Fisetin, a flavonoid, shows similar activity in preclinical work. Navitoclax (ABT-263) is a potent BCL-2/BCL-XL inhibitor that reliably clears senescent cells but causes thrombocytopenia in humans and has been re-engineered as platelet-sparing variants.

Be sober about the human data. Unity Biotechnology's UBX0101 (a local navitoclax-class injection for osteoarthritis knee pain) failed its Phase II in 2020. Senolytics in mice are robust and cross-replicated; senolytics in humans are early, with mostly small open-label studies and mixed signals. The rationale is strong; the clinical proof is incomplete.

title: Nutrient Sensing and Longevity Pathways
description: Insulin/IGF-1, mTOR, AMPK, sirtuins, and caloric restriction

concepts.title: Insulin/IGF-1 Signalling: The Most Conserved Lifespan Switch
concepts.contentHtml:
The single most reproducible genetic intervention in animal aging is downregulation of the insulin/IGF-1 signalling (IIS) cascade. Cynthia Kenyon's 1993 paper showed that daf-2 loss-of-function in C. elegans doubles lifespan and requires the FOXO-orthologue daf-16. The daf-2 receptor is the worm's combined insulin/IGF-1 receptor; reduced signalling lets DAF-16 enter the nucleus and turn on stress-resistance, autophagy, and proteostasis programs.

The pathway is conserved. In Drosophila, mutations in chico (the IRS-1 ortholog) and dilp2 manipulations extend lifespan. In mice, female heterozygous Igf1r-knockouts live ~30% longer (Holzenberger et al. 2003). In humans, the strongest genetic association with extreme longevity yet found is in the FOXO3 locus (Willcox et al., Hawaii / Okinawa cohort) — multiple independent centenarian cohorts confirm the same SNPs.

The mechanism: low IIS lets FOXO induce SOD2, catalase, autophagy genes, and DNA repair genes. The cost: small body size, reduced fertility, and in humans, a real possibility of insulin resistance phenotypes if IIS is blunted globally rather than tissue-specifically. Manipulating IIS pharmacologically remains hard precisely because acute IIS is required for normal glucose homeostasis.

concepts.title: mTOR, Rapamycin and AMPK
concepts.contentHtml:
mTOR is the central nutrient and growth-factor sensor; mTORC1 integrates amino acid availability (via Rag GTPases on the lysosome), growth-factor signalling (via PI3K/AKT), and energy status (via AMPK) to decide whether the cell builds biomass or recycles it. mTORC1 phosphorylates S6K1 and 4E-BP1 to promote translation, blocks ULK1 to inhibit autophagy, and stabilises HIF-1alpha to reroute metabolism. Sustained mTORC1 activity is broadly anti-longevity.

Rapamycin, a soil-bacterium macrolide originally discovered on Easter Island (Rapa Nui), is the cleanest pharmacological tool against mTORC1. The 2009 NIA Interventions Testing Program result — rapamycin extended lifespan in heterogeneous mice even when started at 600 days (~middle age) — was a landmark, the first FDA-approved drug shown unambiguously to extend mammalian lifespan. Matt Kaeberlein's Dog Aging Project tests rapamycin in companion dogs (TRIAD), with human studies in progress in older adults focused on healthspan endpoints.

AMPK is mTOR's antagonist, activated by low energy (high AMP/ATP) and by metformin and exercise. AMPK phosphorylates TSC2 to inhibit mTORC1, activates ULK1 to drive autophagy, and boosts mitochondrial biogenesis via PGC-1alpha. Metformin (Nir Barzilai's TAME trial, lesson 7) is the proposed drug for human translation: cheap, decades-long safety record, plausible mechanism, but its lifespan effect in mice is modest and its anti-aging benefit in non-diabetics in humans remains genuinely uncertain.

concepts.title: Sirtuins, NAD+, and Caloric Restriction
concepts.contentHtml:
The seven mammalian sirtuins (SIRT1-7) are NAD+-dependent deacetylases (and ADP-ribosyltransferases) discovered through Leonard Guarente's work on yeast Sir2 and replicative lifespan. SIRT1 deacetylates p53, FOXO3, PGC-1alpha and histones; SIRT3 is mitochondrial and deacetylates SOD2, MnSOD, and metabolic enzymes; SIRT6 deacetylates H3K9 and H3K56 at telomeres and DNA damage sites and is the only sirtuin whose overexpression extends male mouse lifespan (Kanfi et al., 2012).

Sirtuin activity depends on cellular NAD+, which declines with age. This motivated the NAD+ precursor strategies — NMN and NR — popularised by David Sinclair. Mouse data are real: NMN restores arterial function, exercise endurance, and oocyte quality in old animals. Human data are thinner: small trials show NAD+ rises but downstream functional benefits are modest and inconsistent. Sinclair's claims have outpaced the evidence; treat NAD+-precursor enthusiasm with calibration.

Caloric restriction (CR) — reducing intake by 20-40% without malnutrition — is the most validated lifespan intervention across yeast, worms, flies, and rodents, and the partial mechanism overlaps with all three pathways above (lower IIS, lower mTOR, higher AMPK, higher NAD+/sirtuin activity). The two long-running rhesus monkey CR studies — Wisconsin (positive) and NIA (mostly null on lifespan, positive on healthspan) — disagree, with the modern consensus being that diet composition and baseline obesity status matter as much as caloric quantity. The CALERIE-2 trial in humans showed CR improved cardiovascular and metabolic markers but cannot directly answer the lifespan question.

title: Epigenetic Clocks
description: Methylation-based age prediction from Horvath to GrimAge

concepts.title: Horvath 2013: A Pan-Tissue Methylation Clock
concepts.contentHtml:
Steve Horvath's 2013 paper in Genome Biology was a turning point. He took ~8000 publicly available Illumina 450K arrays spanning 51 tissues and built an elastic-net regression that predicts chronological age from 353 CpG methylation values. Median absolute error is ~3.6 years; the predictor works in essentially every cell type tried, including induced pluripotent stem cells (which it correctly resets to near-zero). The functional form is, in essence:

$$\widehat{\text{age}} \;=\; f\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{353} \beta_i\, m_i\right)$$

where m_i is the methylation beta-value at CpG i, the \beta_i are fitted regression weights, and f is a calibrated transform (logarithmic for ages below 20, linear above). Hannum's clock, published the same year, used 71 CpGs trained on whole blood and is more tissue-restricted but slightly more accurate within its domain.

The clock was a striking demonstration: the epigenome carries a quantitative timer, and a small set of CpGs reads it. Notably, Horvath did not pre-select damage-related sites; the regression simply picked whatever generalised. The clock works on Neanderthal and chimpanzee samples after recalibration, suggesting deep evolutionary conservation of the underlying process — whatever it is.

concepts.title: Second-Generation Clocks: PhenoAge and GrimAge
concepts.contentHtml:
First-generation clocks (Horvath, Hannum) were trained against chronological age. They are excellent age predictors but only modestly correlate with morbidity and mortality — because chronological age is, by construction, only loosely related to biological state.

PhenoAge (Levine et al., 2018) trains in two stages: first fit a 'phenotypic age' from 9 clinical biomarkers (CRP, glucose, albumin, creatinine, white cell count, lymphocyte percent, alkaline phosphatase, RDW, MCV) plus chronological age that predicts mortality, then fit methylation against that synthetic phenotypic age. The result is a 513-CpG clock that predicts all-cause mortality, cancer, cardiovascular disease, and Alzheimer disease much better than Horvath's original.

GrimAge (Lu et al., 2019) goes further. It trains methylation-based surrogates for several plasma proteins (e.g., GDF15, beta-2-microglobulin, PAI-1, cystatin C) plus DNA-methylation-derived smoking pack-years, then combines them in a Cox model for time-to-death. It is currently the strongest methylation predictor of all-cause mortality and the most popular endpoint for clinical longevity trials — DunedinPACE (Belsky et al.) is a related rate-of-aging metric also in wide use. Importantly, second-generation clocks are biologically informative in a way Horvath's original is not: an intervention that lowers GrimAge plausibly hits a real disease pathway, whereas a Horvath-only effect could be epigenetic drift unrelated to health.

concepts.title: What the Clocks Are Actually Measuring
concepts.contentHtml:
What the clocks measure is genuinely uncertain, and the answer matters for interpretation. Three live theories. The damage theory: clocks track accumulated stochastic damage to DNA methylation maintenance — failures of DNMT1, oxidative lesions, replication errors. The developmental program theory: methylation changes are a continuation of the same regulated lineage-specifying program that runs in development; aging is simply the late tail of the developmental clock. The epigenetic noise theory (Vadim Gladyshev, David Sinclair): aging methylation changes are dominated by increasing entropy — loss of a precise youthful pattern rather than acquisition of a specific aged one.

Recent work (Meer et al. 2018; Gladyshev 2021) shows the strongest predictive CpGs are sites with intermediate methylation in young individuals that drift toward 50% (maximum entropy) with age. The Yamanaka-factor partial reprogramming experiments (lesson 6) reset Horvath age dramatically, suggesting at least part of the clock signal is reversible — consistent with the noise-and-erosion picture rather than a pure damage record.

Practically, this matters for trial design. If a clock primarily reads noise, then a successful intervention should not just slow the clock but actively reverse it. If a clock reads damage, reversal should be impossible without molecular repair. The current empirical answer — that some interventions (CR, Yamanaka factors, plasma exchange in mice) move clocks bidirectionally — favours the noise-plus-program view.

title: Reprogramming and Rejuvenation
description: Yamanaka factors, partial reprogramming, and the rejuvenation industry

concepts.title: OSKM: Yamanaka's Four Factors
concepts.contentHtml:
Shinya Yamanaka's 2006 paper showed that four transcription factors — Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc (OSKM) — when introduced into mouse fibroblasts produce induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) functionally equivalent to embryonic stem cells. The 2007 follow-up extended this to human cells. Yamanaka shared the 2012 Nobel with John Gurdon (whose 1962 nuclear-transfer experiments first proved differentiated cells retain a complete genome).

From an aging perspective, the reprogramming process is striking: it does not just change cell identity, it also resets the epigenome. iPSCs derived from old donor fibroblasts have telomeres lengthened toward embryonic values, mitochondrial profiles re-juvenated, and Horvath methylation age near zero. Reprogramming is, mechanistically, the most dramatic rejuvenation event known.

The catch: full reprogramming abolishes cell identity. A Yamanaka-treated hepatocyte becomes an iPSC, not a young hepatocyte. In vivo, sustained OSKM expression causes teratomas and dedifferentiation that is incompatible with tissue function. The original Yamanaka platform is therefore powerful in vitro but immediately unsafe in vivo. The whole modern rejuvenation industry exists to solve this problem.

concepts.title: Partial Reprogramming: Ocampo, Lu, Sinclair
concepts.contentHtml:
Alejandro Ocampo, working in Juan Carlos Izpisua Belmonte's lab, published the foundational partial-reprogramming paper in 2016 (Cell). They engineered a mouse with doxycycline-inducible OSKM and dosed cyclically — a few days on, several days off — rather than continuously. In a progeroid LMNA-mutant background, cyclic OSKM extended lifespan and reduced multi-organ aging phenotypes; in naturally aged wild-type mice, brief pulses improved muscle regeneration and pancreatic beta-cell function without inducing teratomas. The signature insight: identity loss and rejuvenation appear to occur on different timescales, so brief OSKM exposure can rejuvenate without dedifferentiating.

Yuancheng Lu, in David Sinclair's lab, published the 2020 retina paper (Nature) showing that AAV delivery of just OSK (omitting c-Myc, which is the most oncogenic factor) to retinal ganglion cells reversed glaucoma-induced vision loss in mice and partially restored vision in old mice. Methylation age dropped sharply in treated cells. This was the first widely-cited result reframing aging itself as potentially reversible.

Marco Sebastiano, Vittorio Sebastiano and others have explored even shorter exposures and chemical-only cocktails (Sinclair's group reported small-molecule combinations that partially reset Horvath age in 2023). The space is now crowded: Altos Labs launched in 2022 with $3 billion of capital, hiring Belmonte, Sinclair-collaborators, and senior pharma R&D leaders; NewLimit (Brian Armstrong, Blake Byers) targets the same biology with a tighter focus on liver and immune rejuvenation.

concepts.title: Controversies and Limits
concepts.contentHtml:
Three serious caveats temper enthusiasm. First, much of the published partial-reprogramming literature uses progeroid mouse models (LMNA mutants, accelerated-aging genetics) that are not the same biology as normal aging. The cleanest results come from these models; results in unmodified wild-type old mice are real but more modest. Second, there are credible safety concerns: even cyclic OSKM induction has been reported to produce dedifferentiated cells, dysplasia, or carcinoma in some tissues at some doses (Parras et al. and others). Distinguishing rejuvenation from pre-cancerous lineage instability is non-trivial.

Third, the most-publicised claims have outpaced the cleanest evidence. David Sinclair's 'reverse aging' framing in Lifespan (2019) and subsequent media is more confident than the underlying mouse data warrants. The 2023 retraction request and ongoing scrutiny of certain Sinclair-lab papers, plus the broader replication concerns flagged by groups like Vadim Gladyshev's at Harvard, are reminders that the rejuvenation literature has its share of problems.

The honest summary as of 2025: partial reprogramming demonstrably rejuvenates specific tissues in specific mouse models on specific endpoints. It is biologically real and important. It is not yet a clinically deployable therapy, the tumour-risk question is unresolved, and sustained human rejuvenation remains a research aspiration, not a result. Altos and NewLimit will likely produce the first credible early-phase human safety data over 2025-2028; until then, anything stronger is salesmanship.

title: The Modern Frontier
description: TAME, rapamycin, longevity escape velocity, and aging as a disease

concepts.title: TAME, Rapamycin Trials, and the Hard Endpoints Problem
concepts.contentHtml:
TAME (Targeting Aging with Metformin) is Nir Barzilai's pragmatic response to the regulatory problem: the FDA does not recognise 'aging' as an indication, so a trial cannot read out as 'lives longer'. TAME instead enrolls ~3000 adults aged 65-79 and uses a composite endpoint — time to first occurrence of any of cardiovascular events, cancer, dementia, or death. If metformin delays the composite, the inference is that it delays multiple age-related diseases together — a regulatory-accessible proxy for slowing aging itself. As of 2025 the trial is partially funded and partially enrolled; sober observers expect it to take most of the decade.

Rapamycin is the more biologically validated candidate but the harder clinical sell. Matt Kaeberlein's Dog Aging Project ran the TRIAD sub-trial of rapamycin in companion dogs as a cleaner mid-mammal lifespan readout; preliminary cardiac-function and cognitive endpoints look encouraging, with the longer survival readout still maturing. Small human trials (Joan Mannick's PEARL, RTB-101 in elderly flu-vaccine response) hint that low-dose mTOR inhibition can rejuvenate the elderly immune system without serious immunosuppression — but the larger trials needed for outcome-level claims have not yet happened.

The unifying lesson: human aging trials are slow because they need either huge cohorts or composite endpoints. Surrogate markers (epigenetic clocks, GrimAge, frailty indices) are tempting but not yet regulator-accepted. The field's main bottleneck is no longer biological insight but trial throughput.

concepts.title: Longevity Escape Velocity: The Sober View
concepts.contentHtml:
Aubrey de Grey popularised longevity escape velocity (LEV): if life expectancy increases by more than one year per calendar year, an individual already alive can in principle keep ahead of mortality indefinitely. The cartoon is mathematically clean and rhetorically powerful. It also requires assumptions that are not currently met.

The actual rate of life-expectancy gain in high-income countries over the last decade is roughly 0.1-0.2 years per calendar year, and has stalled or reversed in some populations (US since 2014, exacerbated by COVID-19 and opioid mortality). Hitting LEV requires both a sustained order-of-magnitude acceleration of those gains and that the gains target the steep tail of the Gompertz curve at advanced age, where mortality doubling time is short and improvement is hardest.

$$\text{LEV condition:} \quad \frac{d\,\text{LE}}{dt} > 1 \quad (\text{years per year})$$

The de Grey position is that addressing the seven SENS damage categories with maintenance therapies could in principle cross this threshold within decades; he gives 50/50 odds of a 1000-year-old human being alive today. The mainstream biogerontology view (Kirkland, Lopez-Otin, Kaeberlein, Sinclair-when-careful) is that we may plausibly add 5-15 healthy years through hallmark-targeting drugs over the next few decades — meaningful, but not LEV. Treat LEV claims as a useful upper-bound thought experiment, not a forecast.

concepts.title: Aging as a Disease: Regulatory and Ethical Frontier
concepts.contentHtml:
WHO's ICD-11, released for clinical use in 2022, originally introduced an extension code MG2A 'old age' that was sometimes interpreted as a step toward recognising aging as a disease. After backlash from gerontologists who argued this was clinically unhelpful and risked ageist coding, WHO clarified in 2022 that 'old age' is not a primary cause of death. The ICD position remains: aging is the substrate of many diseases but not itself a coded disease.

The FDA's position has evolved. Through 2024-2025 the agency has signalled openness to multi-morbidity composite endpoints (the TAME design), to surrogate biomarkers if they are mechanistically grounded and reproducibly predictive, and to indications framed as 'frailty', 'sarcopenia', or 'aging-related multimorbidity' rather than aging per se. Dale Bredesen and others have pushed for explicit aging-as-disease language; the official position remains cautious. The European Medicines Agency has been more conservative still.

Ethically, the aging-as-disease framing has both supporters (it would unlock R&D investment, insurance coverage, and serious trials) and critics (it risks medicalising normal life, mis-allocates resources, and could deepen inequalities if effective therapies exist but are accessible only to the wealthy). The honest end-state of this lesson: the science is accelerating, the regulatory machinery is moving but slowly, and the ethical conversation is genuinely unsettled. Read primary sources from Lopez-Otin, Kaeberlein, Barzilai, and Gladyshev; treat trade-press 'breakthroughs' with calibrated skepticism.
